proposals.name: Spoken in character versus described from outside
proposals.instruction: Score how far the entry is an utterance a person from the prompt's world would actually say, rather than a third-party description of such a person. 10 = the line is pure in-character speech, with the speaker's own diction, deixis and attitude carried by the words themselves (a quoted brag, threat, complaint, or aside that presupposes a whole speaker). 5 = a noun phrase with some voiced coloring but no clear speaker. 0 = a flat outside-observer label or field-note about the type, with no one speaking, e.g. a bare descriptive noun phrase an anthropologist could have written. Judge only from the wording: presence of second person, contractions, dialect spelling, interjections and vocatives raise the score; bare nominal inventories lower it. Do not reward mere rudeness.
proposals.rationale: The dense-favored side of the slice is dominated by lines that are said, not observed: R56 'Y'all watch this', R60 'Tell you what.', R17 'That's my uncledad!', R10 'I Speak Merican!'. The scorecard-favored side is dominated by outside descriptions of the same stereotype: R37 'Toothless mug shot', R36 'barbecue flavored beard', R25 'WalMart special occasion'. A bank scoring topical fit and stereotype relevance would rate those descriptions equally well while missing that no one is talking.

proposals.name: Self-contained text; no link dependency or off-topic tags
proposals.instruction: Score whether the joke is fully delivered by the visible words, with no reliance on an attached URL, image, or extra hashtags, and no tag clutter beyond the contest hashtag and the host handle. 10 = every element of the humor is recoverable from the text alone and nothing beyond the contest hashtag and host handle is present. 5 = self-contained but carrying one stray extra hashtag or redundant tag. 0 = the line is a caption or setup whose payload evidently sits in a linked image or video, or is buried under additional unrelated hashtags that narrow the audience to a subgroup. Score the dependency, not the topic.
proposals.rationale: The three lowest dense percentiles in the whole slice are exactly the three link-bearing rows: R44 (0.010, 'automotive lawn art' plus a URL), R26 (0.022, 'David Brent in porn flick' plus a URL), R05 (0.049, 'I saw myself on @midnight' plus a URL), and all three are mid-to-high on the card. Rows carrying extra hashtags behave the same way: R23 ('#PointsMe #July4thBirthday', dense 0.042 / card 0.554) and R30 ('#STLCards', dense 0.223 / card 0.926). A criterion bank reading the visible words for wit will happily score these; a reader of the whole item sees an empty or fenced-off line.

proposals.name: Punchline-terminal delivery; tags do not interrupt
proposals.instruction: Score the ordering of the delivery. 10 = the reader meets the joke as a clean uninterrupted phrase and the funniest, most load-bearing word is the last content word, with the contest hashtag and handle trailing behind it as a signature. 5 = the joke is intact but the strongest word sits mid-phrase, or a tag splits the phrase. 0 = administrative material (handle, hashtag) is front-loaded ahead of the joke, or the entry trails off after its own punch, so the line reads as a filed submission rather than a landed line. Score sequence and placement only, not content quality.
proposals.rationale: The split is almost perfectly aligned with word order in this slice. Every dense-favored row places the line first and the tags last: R06 'Up the Holler #RedneckIn3Words @midnight', R12 'Dog: My Copilot #RedneckIn3Words @midnight', R24 'We Were Always Great #AmericaIn4Words @midnight'. Nearly every scorecard-favored row front-loads the tags: R15 '@midnight #RedneckIn3Words Raccoon Defeats Breathalyzer', R33 '@midnight Third tractor dui #RedneckIn3Words', R37 '@midnight Toothless mug shot #RedneckIn3Words'. A bank that extracts the joke text and scores it in isolation is blind to a real property of comic delivery: whether the punch is terminal for the reader.

proposals.name: Minimal-edit hijack of an already-loaded phrase
proposals.instruction: Score the economy of alteration. 10 = a widely known phrase, lyric, slogan or motto is redirected by a single small change, or by no change at all, and the new context does all the work; the machinery is invisible and the line could pass as the original. 5 = a recognizable phrase altered with visible effort but still fluent. 0 = an elaborate constructed mash-up that announces its own cleverness, requiring several substitutions or grafted clauses, and reading as manufactured rather than found. Long, obviously assembled hybrids score low even when the components are apt.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored rows are near-costless redirections: R12 'Dog: My Copilot' (one letter off a bumper sticker), R27 'NASCAR and Chill', R21 'Pass the ammunition', R13 'Don't stop me now.', R32 'Gee, Thanks Obama'. Scorecard-favored rows are visibly assembled: R47 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation', R39 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?', R11 'Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda'. A bank with items for wordplay presence and reference aptness rewards effort per se, which is exactly the wrong sign here.

proposals.name: Alteration yields a second coherent scene, not a sound-alike
proposals.instruction: Score whether the wordplay produces a genuinely new, imaginable situation as well as a resemblance. 10 = after the substitution the phrase depicts a specific second scene or claim that stands on its own and is funny even to someone who half-remembers the source. 5 = the second reading exists but is thin or merely gestural. 0 = the change is only phonetic or orthographic; the altered token points at a topic without asserting anything about it, so nothing new can be pictured. Ask concretely: can I describe what is happening in the joke? If the only answer is a restatement of the pun, score low.
proposals.rationale: R03 'Judge Dread' (dense 0.037 / card 0.613) and R50 'All the White Moves' (dense 0.081 / card 0.625) are clean surface swaps that assert nothing; nothing can be pictured beyond the resemblance. Contrast R12 'Dog: My Copilot', which conjures an entire truck cab, and R42 'Mother visits me, stays FOREVER', which conjures a whole occupied house. A bank that checks whether a pun is present and well-formed cannot distinguish a pun that opens a scene from one that only rhymes.

proposals.name: Reliance on franchise scaffolding: sequel numbers, colons, subtitles
proposals.instruction: Score inversely to how much of the construction is carried by borrowed title furniture. 0-3 = the entry leans on sequel numerals, colons, subtitles, or roman numerals to hold the joke together, so the structure comes pre-supplied by the source and the contributed content is a single grafted word or phrase. 5 = one such device used but the contributed material carries the line. 10 = no borrowed scaffolding; the entry stands as a complete phrase whose shape the writer chose. Judge the presence and load-bearing role of the furniture, not the topic.
proposals.rationale: The scaffolding-heavy rows cluster on the scorecard-high side: R53 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz', R47 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation', R52 'Star Wars VII: series finale', R48 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders'. None of the dense-favored rows uses a sequel number or subtitle colon in this way. A criterion bank rewarding recognizable-title usage and structural completeness will score the furniture itself, treating a colon as evidence of craft.

proposals.name: Breadth of prerequisite knowledge; not fandom or celebrity gated
proposals.instruction: Score how wide the audience is that can get the joke with no lookup. 10 = the reference is a near-universal experience, object or fear needing no fandom, no sports allegiance, no celebrity gossip and no regional insider knowledge. 5 = mainstream but generational or national. 0 = the line is inert unless the reader follows a specific franchise, team, or performer's career, or shares a private grievance about one named individual. Rate the gate, not whether you personally passed it.
proposals.rationale: Every scorecard-favored scary-story row is knowledge-gated: R43 'Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie.', R57 'Star Wars 7 With JarJar.', R52 'Star Wars VII: series finale', R26 'David Brent in porn flick', R30 'Cubs Win the World Series #STLCards', R04 'Thrice Oscar nominee Bradley Cooper.' The dense-favored scary-story rows are ungated dread: R42 'Mother visits me, stays FOREVER', R54 'Accident causes sphincter control loss', R40 'My neighbor is a Clown!'. A bank that credits topical relevance and reference specificity treats a narrow reference as a strength.

proposals.name: Not the first answer the prompt hands everyone
proposals.instruction: Score inversely to predictability. Imagine a thousand people answering this exact prompt. 10 = fewer than a handful would land on this; the angle had to be found. 5 = a plausible but not automatic answer. 0 = the single most obvious pairing the prompt suggests, the answer that arrives before any thinking, such that the same submission would appear dozens of times. Judge inevitability given the prompt, independent of whether the joke is well made. A technically flawless but foregone entry scores 0-2.
proposals.rationale: R18 'Kill Bill of Rights' (dense 0.029 / card 0.775) is the single most foregone GOP-movie pun available; R52 and R57 are the era's most-submitted scary-story reference, differing only in spelling of the same Star Wars beat, and both sit high on the card (0.980, 0.792) and near the floor on the dense side (0.135, 0.179). A criterion bank has no notion of crowding: it scores each item as if it were the only entry, so an inevitable joke and a found one look identical to it.

proposals.name: Constraint-aware wordcraft: fusing words to fit the budget
proposals.instruction: Score how far the prompt's word budget is treated as material for the joke rather than a container to fill. 10 = the writer coins, fuses, contracts or elides to make the count itself do comic work: a portmanteau, a hyphen-chain, or a clipped dialect spelling that both obeys the count and is the joke. 5 = clean, exact compliance with no play. 0 = the count is ignored, padded, or met with unremarkable filler. For prompts with no stated count, score compression instead: whether every word is load-bearing.
proposals.rationale: The dense-favored side keeps gaming the counter: R09 'Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie' fuses two hyphen-chains to make four words hold six, R17 coins 'uncledad', R01 'Meth'd up Mondays' verbs a noun, R10 clips 'Merican'. Nothing on the scorecard-high side does this; R37 'Toothless mug shot' and R33 'Third tractor dui' merely occupy three slots. A bank almost certainly has a compliance item, which scores both as fully compliant and cannot see that in one case the compliance is the punchline.

proposals.name: No self-gloss; the joke is not explained in the line
proposals.instruction: Score inversely to how much the entry explains itself. 10 = the joke is stated once and trusted; no parenthetical, no appositive, no clarifying rider. 5 = a small redundancy. 0 = the line contains its own footnote, spelling out the pun, the arithmetic, or the referent, so the reader is told the joke rather than getting it. Parenthetical asides that add a further turn are not glosses and should not be penalized; only explanatory ones count.
proposals.rationale: R59 'Everybody, my bruncle! (brother + uncle)' hands over its own derivation, while the unglossed R17 'That's my uncledad!' makes the same move and sits far higher on the dense side (0.855 vs 0.542). R19 '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' spells out its own arithmetic and is one of the sharpest card-over-dense rows (card 0.907 / dense 0.113). A bank with items for clarity or intelligibility will actively reward the gloss, since the glossed version is easier to understand.

proposals.name: List whose final item swerves against the earlier ones
proposals.instruction: For entries built as a list or triple, score whether the last item breaks the pattern the earlier items set, retroactively reframing them. 10 = the first items establish a comfortable category and the final item lands in a different register, turning the list into an argument. 5 = a list with a rhythmically satisfying but categorically flat close. 0 = an undifferentiated inventory in which the items are interchangeable and the order does not matter. Entries that are not lists should be scored on whether their final word similarly redirects what came before.
proposals.rationale: R45 'Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy' sets up three tailgate nouns and closes with a political indictment; R29 'Guns, No Abortions' sets a pairing that turns on the reader. Both sit dense-high with low card scores (0.699/0.194 and 0.848/0.159). By contrast R34 'Corn syrup and salt' and R49-style flat inventories are interchangeable lists. A bank with a wordplay or list-structure item scores the surface form, not whether the last slot does work.

proposals.name: Reframes the prompt instead of answering it
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry treats the prompt as a question to be filled in or as a premise to be challenged. 10 = the line answers with a question, rebuttal, reply-fragment or refusal that recasts the prompt itself, so the humor is about the prompt's assumption rather than about its subject. 5 = a straight answer with an ironic tilt. 0 = a compliant slot-filling answer that accepts the premise entirely. Meta moves that are merely off-topic, rather than turned against the premise, score low.
proposals.rationale: R02 'How Free Are You?' answers a describe-America prompt with an interrogation of it; R51 'But we're we really?' is a reply-shaped fragment that presupposes and rebuts a prior boast; R08 'Need To Get Out' converts the prompt into a complaint; R24 'We Were Always Great' turns it into a contested political claim. All four are dense-high with card scores between 0.096 and 0.238. A bank scoring topical fit and prompt compliance reads a question or a rebuttal as an incomplete answer and marks it down.

proposals.name: Target reassignment: the joke redirects at a new group
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry aims its subject at an unexpected target rather than the one the prompt nominates, in a way that makes the reassignment itself the point. 10 = the line takes the prompt's stereotype and attaches it to a group, faction or the reader's own tribe that the prompt did not invite, so the reader has to recompute who is being described. 5 = a mild widening of the target. 0 = the joke lands exactly where the prompt pointed. Score the redirection, not the political stance, and not how offensive the content is.
proposals.rationale: The dense-favored side keeps reassigning: R55 'Proud Republican Tools' and R32 'Gee, Thanks Obama' and R41 'Not my president!' all convert a regional-stereotype prompt into partisan identification, and R28 'Democrats America's Retarded People' aims a national prompt at a party. The card scores these among the lowest in the slice (0.304, 0.480, 0.147, 0.047). This looks like a bank that treats prompt-appropriate subject matter as a positive and political charge as a negative, exactly inverting the move.

proposals.name: Implied off-screen story the line makes the reader complete
proposals.instruction: Score the amount of unstated narrative the phrase forces the reader to construct. 10 = the words are an innocuous fragment, but reading them the reader involuntarily supplies what happened just before and what is about to happen, and the unsaid part is the joke. 5 = the line implies a situation but states most of it. 0 = the line is a static label or snapshot, fully consumed on reading, with nothing before or after it. Explicit description of the funny event scores low; a line that makes the reader do the imagining scores high.
proposals.rationale: R56 'Y'all watch this' contains no joke at all on its face and yet delivers an entire impending catastrophe; R60 'Tell you what.' delivers a whole character from a discourse marker; R42 'Mother visits me, stays FOREVER' implies years of siege; R31 'Father brother in-law' implies a family tree. All are dense-high with card scores 0.051-0.407. The scorecard-favored R37 'Toothless mug shot' and R36 'barbecue flavored beard' are complete snapshots with nothing offscreen. A bank scoring imagery vividness or specificity prefers the snapshot.

proposals.name: Transgression carried by construction, not by a shock token
proposals.instruction: For entries with taboo, gross or cruel content, score whether the transgression is delivered through committed construction or merely named. 10 = the taboo element is embedded in a built line with rhythm, voice or a turn, so the shock arrives as the consequence of the joke's shape. 5 = shocking content with adequate but unremarkable phrasing. 0 = a taboo noun is simply placed next to the prompt's subject and left there, with the offensive word doing all the work and no construction around it. Entries with no transgressive content should be scored 5 as not applicable; do not reward or punish offensiveness itself.
proposals.rationale: The dense model is plainly not shock-averse: R54 'Accident causes sphincter control loss' (dense 0.978) and R28 (dense 0.846) are both transgressive and both dense-high. What it discounts is the bare taboo noun: R07 'Family reunion Rohypnol' (dense 0.164 / card 0.990) and R38 'Frenching your sister' (dense 0.225 / card 0.806) name the taboo and stop. R20 'Meth, Meth, Meth' (dense 0.838 / card 0.100) uses the same drug reference but builds it into a repetition bit and lands on the opposite side. A bank with items for boldness or edginess counts the taboo token and cannot see whether anything was built around it.

proposals.name: Administrative prefix versus trailing signature placement of handle and hashtag
proposals.instruction: Score only WHERE the contest hashtag and the host handle sit relative to the joke text; do not judge whether this is good or bad, and do not let the joke itself influence you. 10 = all administrative tokens (handle, contest hashtag) are front-loaded before the joke body, so the reader meets routing material first. 5 = tags are split around the body, or one leads and one trails. 0 = the joke body comes first and every tag trails behind it as a signature. Count position only. An entry with excellent or terrible wording gets the same score if the layout is the same.
proposals.rationale: This is close to a perfect separator in the slice and is pure layout. Every strongly dense-favored row trails its tags: R15 'Up the Holler  #RedneckIn3Words @midnight' (0.961/0.363), R37 'We Were Always Great  #AmericaIn4Words @midnight' (0.988/0.223), R12 (0.968/0.480). Nearly every scorecard-favored row front-loads them: R06 '@midnight #RedneckIn3Words Raccoon Defeats Breathalyzer' (0.284/0.998), R47 (0.164/0.990), R10 (0.270/0.904), R14 (0.147/0.652). Tellingly, the three scorecard-favored rows that do NOT front-load (R04 0.370, R05 0.368, R19 0.453) are the three highest dense percentiles inside that whole group. Whether a writer types the tag before or after the line is a keyboard habit, not a property of the joke; it is plausibly a fingerprint of format practice, which is why I tag it mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (habitual @midnight entrant versus drive-by submitter)

proposals.name: Capitalization styling of the entry body
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of non-default capitalization in the joke body only, ignoring hashtags and handles. 10 = every content word is capitalized as if the entry were a title or headline, or a whole word is set in ALL CAPS for emphasis. 5 = first word capitalized plus one proper noun, standard sentence casing. 0 = the body is entirely lowercase or begins lowercase. This is a typographic count, not an assessment: do not reward or penalize the style, and do not consider whether the capitalization suits the joke.
proposals.rationale: The two sides of the slice are styled differently at the level of shift-key use alone. Title-cased bodies sit dense-high: R07 'How Free Are You?', R44 'Need To Get Out', R37 'We Were Always Great', R13 'Country Music Twang', R54 'I Speak Merican!', plus caps-emphasis in R17 'stays FOREVER' and R48 'ACTUAL Sister Wives'. Lowercase-running bodies sit dense-low and card-high: R14 'Toothless mug shot' (0.147/0.652), R52 'barbecue flavored beard' (0.260/0.762), R10 'Third tractor dui' (0.270/0.904), R50 'automotive lawn art' (0.010/0.804), R31 'multiple COPS appearances'. Capitalization carries no comic information here, so any model tracking it is tracking a typing habit.
proposals.upstream_parent: composition habit: whether the writer treats the entry as a titled unit or as a running phrase

proposals.name: Presence of an attached URL or media pointer
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the item consists of, or points to, material outside the text. 10 = the item carries a t.co or other URL, or otherwise explicitly refers the reader to an attached picture, video or linked page. 5 = a quoted or reported fragment implying an external source but with no link present. 0 = plain text with no link and no pointer. Score only the presence and prominence of the pointer. Do not attempt to judge whether the link helps or hurts the entry, and do not speculate about what is on the other end.
proposals.rationale: The three link-bearing rows are the three lowest dense percentiles in the entire 60-row slice, and all three sit mid-to-high on the card: R50 'automotive lawn art http://t.co/...' (0.010/0.804), R35 'David Brent in porn flick ... https://t.co/...' (0.022/0.591), R26 'I saw myself on @midnight ... https://t.co/...' (0.049/0.554). A model can key on the literal 't.co' string without any understanding of the joke, which makes this a textual fingerprint of how the tweet was composed rather than of what it says. I tag mixed because the same parent (the joke actually living in an attached image) can plausibly also mean the visible text really is a weaker standalone entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: composition mode: the entry was authored as a photo or link tweet from a client that appends a URL

proposals.name: Extra hashtags beyond the contest tag
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of hashtag material that is not the contest hashtag. 10 = two or more additional hashtags are present, including tags that address a fan community, a sports allegiance, a personal occasion, or the contest's own scoring culture. 5 = exactly one additional hashtag. 0 = only the contest hashtag appears. Count tags; do not assess whether they are relevant, witty, or annoying, and do not let the joke's content affect the score.
proposals.rationale: R01 carries '#PointsMe #July4thBirthday' alongside the contest tag and sits at dense 0.042 with card 0.542; R53 carries '#STLCards' and sits at dense 0.223 with card 0.926. In both cases the extra tags do no comic work at all: they address people outside the contest. The conjectured parent (an author seeking amplification or speaking to a private circle) has no plausible path to making the entry itself funnier, so I tag it unmixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience and following effects: the author is recruiting attention or addressing a subgroup outside the contest

proposals.name: Body length and token count
proposals.instruction: Score the sheer size of the joke body, excluding tags and handles. 10 = seven or more words, or the body runs past roughly forty characters, or it contains bracketed or appended clauses adding bulk. 5 = four to five words. 0 = three words or fewer and under roughly twenty characters. Measure length only. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate to the prompt, whether the entry is concise or padded, or whether any word is wasted.
proposals.rationale: Length tracks the split without tracking the joke. The longest bodies in the slice are scorecard-favored: R18 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?' (0.132/0.936), R04 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders' (0.370/0.939), R45 '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' (0.113/0.907). The shortest are dense-favored: R03 'Tell you what.' (0.740/0.257), R15 'Up the Holler' (0.961/0.363). Because the word budget is fixed by the contest and the contests are unevenly represented in the slice, a length feature is largely reading off which night an item came from. I tag mixed since economy under a stated word cap is also a real part of doing these prompts well.
proposals.upstream_parent: which contest container the item belongs to, since each night's prompt sets its own word budget

proposals.name: Borrowed-title template markers: colons, numerals, subtitles
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the entry's visible structure is a film or franchise title skeleton. 10 = the entry contains a colon-plus-subtitle, a sequel numeral or roman numeral, or is otherwise recognizably shaped as an existing title with a slot substituted. 5 = a recognizable title is used but with no numeral, colon or subtitle furniture. 0 = no title template of any kind. Score the presence of the template machinery only. Do not judge whether the title is well chosen, whether the substitution is funny, or whether the reference is apt.
proposals.rationale: Every row carrying this furniture sits scorecard-high and dense-low: R04 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders' (0.370/0.939), R05 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation' (0.368/0.885), R21 'Star Wars VII: series finale' (0.135/0.980), R32 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz' (0.179/0.792), R55 'Kill Bill of Rights' (0.029/0.775), R58 'Judge Dread' (0.037/0.613). No dense-favored row uses it. Since #GOP_Movies and the movie-flavored scary-story entries structurally require a title, this channel is close to a container indicator wearing the costume of a craft feature: a colon is not wit. I tag mixed because contest genre also legitimately determines what a good entry looks like.
proposals.upstream_parent: which contest container the item belongs to (a title-mashup night versus a voice or list night)

proposals.name: Unprompted partisan content the contest did not request
proposals.instruction: Score how much explicitly partisan material appears that the contest hashtag itself did not call for. 10 = named politicians, parties, factions, slogans or hot-button policy nouns are central to an entry whose prompt is not about politics. 5 = a faint political tint, or partisan content in a contest that explicitly asks for it. 0 = no partisan content. Judge only the amount and prominence of partisan reference. You must not judge whether the politics is fair, sharp, offensive, or whether you agree with it, and you must not treat political content as either a merit or a defect.
proposals.rationale: Where the prompt is apolitical, partisan imports are uniformly dense-high and card-low: R02 'Democrats America's Retarded People' (0.846/0.047), R09 'Proud Republican Tools' (0.873/0.304), R20 'Not my president!' (0.615/0.147), R49 'Guns, No Abortions' (0.848/0.159), R12 'Gee, Thanks Obama' (0.968/0.480). Where the prompt requests politics (#GOPMovies) the same material is card-high: R39 (0.897), R28 (0.978). The two models are responding to the presence of a political register in opposite directions, which is a property of the readers rather than of the joke.
proposals.upstream_parent: topic composition of the night's prompt combined with the receiving side's sensitivity to political material

proposals.name: Taboo, slur and bodily-shock lexical content
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of taboo lexical material present. 10 = a slur, a reference to drugging, sexual assault, incest, or an explicit bodily-function term appears. 5 = a milder vice or drug reference, or crude but non-taboo content. 0 = nothing a broadcaster would flag. Count the presence and strength of the taboo tokens only. You must not judge whether the transgression is earned, well constructed, funny, or gratuitous, and you must not raise or lower the score for your own reaction to it.
proposals.rationale: Taboo tokens move scores hard and in both directions, which is exactly the signature of a nuisance rather than a quality dimension. The slur in R02 pairs with the lowest card percentile in the slice (0.047) despite dense 0.846, while the drugging reference in R47 'Family reunion Rohypnol' pairs with almost the highest card percentile (0.990) despite dense 0.164; R56 'Frenching your sister' is 0.225/0.806 and R17 'Accident causes sphincter control loss' is 0.978/0.493. Nothing about how well built these lines are explains that spread; the identity of the taboo word does. The parent here is reader sensitivity, which has no path to making the entry itself better, so I tag it unmixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: sensitivity of the receiving side (audience and annotators) to offensive material, independent of construction

proposals.name: Date-stamped topicality: tells that pin the item to a news cycle
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the text is pinned to a specific moment. 10 = the entry names a then-imminent release, an award season, a playoff or election that was live at the time, or states a year outright, so a reader could date the item from the text. 5 = a reference to a public figure whose salience is period-bound but not tied to an event. 0 = no temporal anchor; the text would read identically in any year. Score datability only. Do not judge whether the topicality makes the joke better or more stale.
proposals.rationale: The datable rows cluster on the scorecard-favored side: R21 'Star Wars VII: series finale' (0.135/0.980) and R60 'Star Wars 7 With JarJar.' (0.275/0.816) both sit in a pre-release window, R53 'Cubs Win the World Series' (0.223/0.926) sits in a specific season, R32 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz' (0.179/0.792) in a primary, R19 'Thrice Oscar nominee Bradley Cooper' (0.453/0.951) in an award cycle, and R01 says '2013' outright. The dense-favored rows are almost all undatable. Submission timing is an unseen upstream factor, and these phrases are its visible fingerprint; I tag mixed because being current is also part of what made an entry land on the night.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing: which night's contest this was and what was in the news that week

proposals.name: Crowded-lane fingerprint: most available take, or marked variant of one
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry reads as occupying a lane that many other entrants would independently have occupied for this same prompt. 10 = the entry is either the single most immediately available pairing the prompt suggests, or a near-duplicate of such a beat carrying a small differentiating rider (an appended parenthetical, a sequel number, a subtitle, a respelling) that reads as an attempt to distinguish it from a take already made. 5 = a common register but no evident duplicate. 0 = a lane it is hard to imagine anyone else independently entering. Score availability and duplicate-marking only. Do not judge originality as a virtue or predictability as a fault; you are estimating how crowded the lane looks, not how good the entry is.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains direct textual evidence of crowding: three separate rows in the same scary-story contest work the identical Star Wars / Jar Jar beat (R21 0.135/0.980, R23 0.172/0.912, R60 0.275/0.816), and two rows in the same GOP contest work the identical 'Angry Men' beat (R04 0.370/0.939, R45 0.113/0.907). Every one of them is scorecard-favored and dense-disfavored. The differentiating riders are visible on their faces: ': The Contenders', '(and one woman)', 'With JarJar.'. R55 'Kill Bill of Rights' (0.029/0.775) is the most available pun the prompt admits. A criterion bank scores each item as though it were the only submission, so it cannot see the container; but position in the stream is an unseen upstream factor, not a property of the line, which is why it belongs here rather than in the bank. I tag mixed because arriving late plausibly also pushes an author toward genuinely more original writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream: how early or late the item was submitted into an already-crowded container

proposals.name: Clean, recognizable-source pun substitution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet is built on a single well-known named phrase (movie title, ad slogan, book/show title, idiom) altered by one clean, minimal substitution that snaps cleanly back onto the recognized original; score 5 if the source is only loosely recognizable or the substitution is clumsy; score 0 if the tweet has no identifiable pre-existing source text being punned on at all.
proposals.rationale: R20 ('Kill Bill of Rights'), R45 ('Tastes great, less filling'), R53 ('Judge Dread'), and R58 ('All the White Moves') are all clean substitutions into a recognizable title/slogan; the scorecard ranks all four near the top (card_pct .775-.980) while the dense model ranks them near the bottom (dense_pct .029-.233), suggesting the scorecard rewards this structural move heavily even when little else is added.

proposals.name: Deadpan understatement, punchline left unspoken
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet states a plain, flat fact or command with zero explanation and the reader must supply the comedic inference entirely themselves; score 5 if some inference is required but the tweet also nudges the reader toward the joke; score 0 if the tweet spells out its own comedic logic explicitly, leaving nothing for the reader to infer.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('Y'all watch this', dense .767/card .252), R31 ('Need To Get Out', dense .897/card .145), and R52 ('Tell you what.', dense .740/card .257) are all terse, unexplained lines the dense model ranks far above the scorecard, suggesting withheld punchlines are underweighted by the scorecard.

proposals.name: Adapts a live contemporary meme or catchphrase
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet is instantly recognizable as a reuse of a specific, currently-circulating meme, bumper-sticker phrase, or internet/pop catchphrase (not a movie/book/show title) repurposed to fit the contest theme; score 5 if the phrase is a stock idiom with only weak meme/pop-culture currency; score 0 if the wording contains no trace of any pre-existing meme or catchphrase.
proposals.rationale: R41 ('Dog: My Copilot', dense .924/card .213), R57 ('NASCAR and Chill', dense .953/card .324), and R54 ('Gee, Thanks Obama', dense .968/card .480) each repurpose a live meme/bumper-sticker phrase; dense rates them near the top while card rates them mid-low, unlike the title-pun cases in A01.

proposals.name: Blunt partisan/taboo claim, no comic cushioning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet makes a sharp partisan or socially taboo claim stated as a flat assertion with no joke structure, wordplay, or softening device wrapped around it; score 5 if taboo/partisan content is present but cushioned by a pun or qualifier; score 0 if the tweet contains no partisan or taboo content at all.
proposals.rationale: R19 ('Democrats America's Retarded People', dense .846/card .047), R59 ('Guns, No Abortions', dense .848/card .159), and R39 ('We Were Always Great', dense .988/card .223) are blunt partisan/taboo assertions the dense model rates very highly and the scorecard rates near the bottom.

proposals.name: Wordplay left unglossed, not self-explained
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet contains a blend-word, portmanteau, or pun and does NOT explain or unpack it, trusting the reader to parse it unaided; score 5 if there is a light gloss; score 0 if the tweet explicitly spells out the mechanism of its own wordplay, e.g. a parenthetical explaining a blended word.
proposals.rationale: R13 ('That's my uncledad!', unglossed, dense .855) scores far higher on dense than R22 ('Everybody, my bruncle! (brother+uncle)', explicitly glossed, dense .542) even though both use the same blend-word device and both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting spelling out the mechanism weakens a joke the dense model would otherwise favor more.

proposals.name: Consistent in-character dialect/persona voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entire tweet is phrased as a first-person or address-form line in a sustained, distinct social voice/dialect appropriate to the contest's target persona; score 5 if a persona voice is present but inconsistent or thin; score 0 if the tweet is written in neutral, voiceless description with no persona.
proposals.rationale: R24 ('I Speak 'Merican!', dense .929/card .365), R42 ('Up the Holler', dense .961/card .363), and R52 ('Tell you what.', dense .740/card .257) are persona-voiced lines the dense model consistently ranks high relative to the scorecard.

proposals.name: Payoff lands complete within minimal word count
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet is 4 words or fewer (excluding hashtag/handle) and the joke is fully self-contained at that length with nothing missing; score 5 for roughly 5-8 words; score 0 if the tweet needs many words or clauses to build up to its point.
proposals.rationale: R37 ('Meth, Meth, Meth', 3 words, dense .838/card .100), R60 ('Meth'd up Mondays', 3 words, dense .860/card .299), and R16 ('Pass the ammunition', 3 words, dense .926/card .449) are extremely short, complete-feeling lines the dense model favors heavily over the scorecard.

proposals.name: Focus undiluted by self-promo or meta reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet is entirely devoted to the joke text itself, with no extra hashtags beyond the contest tag, no embedded links/images, and no reference to the show, the contest, or the act of appearing on it; score 0 if the tweet spends part of its content on extra hashtags, a link, or a meta-reference to the show/contest.
proposals.rationale: R11 ('I saw myself on @midnight' plus a link, dense .049/card .554), R47 ('Twerking Ever Since 2013 #PointsMe #July4thBirthday', dense .042/card .542), and R25 ('Cubs Win the World Series ... #STLCards', dense .029/card .775) are all padded with extra hashtags, a link, or a self-referential mention of the show, and are exactly the items where the scorecard rates them high while dense does not.

proposals.name: Asyndetic noun-list cadence for comic rhythm
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet is a list of two or more concrete nouns/noun phrases strung together without conjunctions, producing a rhythmic, escalating cadence; score 0 if the tweet is a single continuous clause with no list structure.
proposals.rationale: R43 ('Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups', dense .934/card .245), R50 ('Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy', dense .699/card .194), and R27 ('Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie', dense .873/card .304) are pure asyndetic noun-list entries the dense model rates well above the scorecard.

proposals.name: Pun stacks two or more meanings at once
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet's central wordplay simultaneously activates two distinct meanings or reference registers at once (e.g. a title pun that ALSO carries a separate topical/political meaning); score 5 if there is a pun but only a single register of meaning; score 0 if there is no pun or double meaning present.
proposals.rationale: R20 ('Kill Bill of Rights' stacks a movie-title pun with a constitutional register) and R55 ('What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?' stacks a movie-title pun with a healthcare-policy jab) both stack two registers, as does R28 ('Proud Republican Tools', stacking literal and idiomatic senses of 'tools'); these appear on both sides of the disagreement, marking double-stacking as a distinct axis worth isolating from single-register puns.

proposals.name: Invents a vivid, self-contained mini-scenario
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet depicts a specific invented event or mini-narrative (an action happening to a particular subject) rather than a static label or noun phrase; score 0 if the tweet is just a static noun phrase or label with no depicted event.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('Raccoon Defeats Breathalyzer', dense .284/card .998), R49 ('Accident causes sphincter control loss', dense .978/card .493), and R56 ('Mother visits me, stays FOREVER', dense .966/card .407) all invent a small vivid scene rather than stating a static label, and appear on both sides of the disagreement.

proposals.name: Bodily or sexual taboo as comic engine
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet's humor is generated primarily through graphic bodily, sexual, or otherwise physically taboo/gross-out content; score 5 if taboo content is present but secondary to another device; score 0 if the tweet contains no bodily/sexual/taboo material.
proposals.rationale: R32 ('Frenching your sister', dense .225/card .806), R36 ('Family reunion Rohypnol', dense .164/card .990), and R49 ('Accident causes sphincter control loss', dense .978/card .493) all use bodily/sexual taboo as the comic engine and appear on both sides of the disagreement, suggesting the current instrument may be scoring this device inconsistently.

proposals.name: Alliteration, rhyme, or rhythmic sound-play
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet uses clear alliteration, internal rhyme, or a marked rhythmic/metrical pattern in its wording, independent of any title pun; score 0 if the wording has no notable sonic patterning.
proposals.rationale: R60 ('Meth'd up Mondays', alliteration/rhyme echoing 'Manic Monday', dense .860/card .299), R42 ('Up the Holler', rhythmic phrase, dense .961/card .363), and R33 ('barbecue flavored beard', alliterative, dense .260/card .762) show sonic wordplay recurring on both sides of the disagreement.

proposals.name: Joke mechanism matches the hashtag's named genre
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the specific comedic technique used (e.g. genuine fright/unease for a 'scary story' tag, a plausible-sounding title for a 'movies' tag) is exactly what the contest's named theme calls for, such that the joke would lose its point if pasted into a different hashtag's contest; score 0 if the tweet's content is generic and could be pasted under an unrelated contest hashtag with no loss of sense or effect.
proposals.rationale: Within the same #Scary_Story_In_5_Words tag, R56 ('Mother visits me, stays FOREVER', genuinely unsettling, dense .966/card .407) is dense-favored while R25 ('Cubs Win the World Series ... #STLCards', a sports non-sequitur with no fright content, dense .029/card .775) and R48 ('Star Wars VII: series finale', a movie pun with no scary content, dense .135/card .980) are card-favored despite delivering none of the named genre's actual mechanism.

proposals.name: Anchors on a loaded proper-noun or brand reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet's payoff depends on naming a specific real institution, brand, media franchise, or public figure whose connotation the reader is assumed to already know, used to instantly import social meaning; score 5 if a proper noun is present but not load-bearing; score 0 if the tweet contains no proper nouns/brand names at all.
proposals.rationale: R38 ('ACTUAL Sister Wives', dense .725/card .123) and R34 ('WalMart special occasion', dense .279/card .887) both anchor on a specific named brand/franchise to import instant social connotation, appearing on opposite sides of the disagreement and marking proper-noun grounding as distinct from generic wordplay.

proposals.name: Extra hashtags or links beyond the single contest tag
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much content in the tweet is devoted to hashtags, links, or handles OTHER than the single required contest hashtag and the @midnight mention: 0 = no additional hashtags/links/handles present at all; 10 = multiple additional hashtags and/or an embedded link are present. This is an extent measure only -- do not judge whether the extra material is good or bad for the joke.
proposals.rationale: R37 ('#PointsMe #July4thBirthday') and R55 ('#STLCards') attach extra hashtags unrelated to the joke; R04 and R05 attach embedded links. These are visible submission-behavior tells, not evidence about how funny the line itself is, yet they could plausibly sway a judge's attention.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's self-promotion / engagement-seeking submission practice (adding extra tags/links to attract attention beyond the contest itself)

proposals.name: Handle/hashtag block placed before vs after the joke text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the tweet's @midnight mention and contest hashtag appears BEFORE the joke text (as a leading block) rather than after it: 0 = all handle/hashtag material trails after the joke text; 10 = all handle/hashtag material leads before the joke text. Score only the position of this boilerplate, never whether the joke itself is good.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('@midnight #AmericaIn4Words Tastes great, less filling') and R09 ('@midnight Third tractor dui #RedneckIn3Words') lead with the boilerplate, while R40 ('Need To Get Out #AmericaIn4Words @midnight') and R47 ('Pass the ammunition #RedneckIn3Words @midnight') trail it -- a pure formatting habit that a card built from content-focused criteria should not be swayed by, but a judge skimming past a leading tag block first could be primed differently than one reading the joke first.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Irregular double-space runs around hashtag or handle
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many places in the tweet contain two or more consecutive spaces (irregular whitespace) around the hashtag, handle, or joke text: 0 = perfectly single-spaced throughout; 10 = multiple double(or more)-space runs present. Score only the presence of the whitespace pattern, not whether it makes the tweet look better or worse.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('@midnight  #AmericaIn4Words  Tastes great, less filling') and R47 ('Pass the ammunition  #RedneckIn3Words @midnight') both carry double-space runs, likely a mechanical artifact of a particular submission client or copy-paste habit rather than anything about the joke's quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Formal closing punctuation (period or question mark) on the joke line
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the core joke phrase is closed with formal terminal punctuation (a period or question mark) as if it were a complete written sentence: 0 = no terminal punctuation on the joke phrase; 10 = the joke phrase ends with a period or question mark. Score only presence of the punctuation mark, not whether the sentence reads well.
proposals.rationale: R26 ('Don't stop me now.'), R14 ('Tell you what.'), R43 ('But we're we really?'), and R46 ('How Free Are You?') all close with formal terminal punctuation, a stylistic habit some authors carry into every sentence they write online, which could be a proxy for a more literate/practiced writer rather than for a funnier line.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's general writing register / formality habit, independent of comedic content

proposals.name: Hashtag capitalization matches the show's official CamelCase style
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how closely the tweet's hashtag capitalization matches a clean CamelCase rendering of the contest name (e.g. #ScaryStoryIn5Words): 0 = hashtag is all lowercase or otherwise clearly deviates from CamelCase; 10 = hashtag exactly matches clean CamelCase capitalization. Score only the capitalization match, not whether the joke is funny.
proposals.rationale: R18 uses '#gopmovies' in all lowercase while R28 uses '#GOPmovies' and R41 uses '#GOPMOVIES' -- all deviating differently from clean CamelCase -- versus rows like R56 that render '#GOPMovies' in exact CamelCase; this typing-convention fidelity looks like a marker of practice/familiarity rather than of the joke's own quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's platform experience / familiarity with the show's hashtag convention (a 'regular' who has typed this hashtag many times, vs. a newer or less careful entrant)

proposals.name: Minimal fill-in-the-blank answer vs. fuller narrated sentence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet consists ONLY of a minimal noun-phrase or short-phrase answer to the prompt with no surrounding narration, commentary, or connecting words, versus how much it reads as a fuller, grammatically complete narrated sentence: 0 = fully narrated sentence with subject, verb, and connective grammar; 10 = a bare minimal phrase/answer with no narrative framing. Score only the structural minimalism, not whether the content is clever.
proposals.rationale: R40 ('Need To Get Out') and R47 ('Pass the ammunition') are bare minimal answers with no narration, while R43 ('But we're we really?') and R27 ('Thrice Oscar nominee Bradley Cooper.') read as fuller narrated sentences; this structural choice looks like a format-practice tell that could be conflated with joke quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice/experience with this specific fill-in-the-blank party-game format (regulars learn to answer tersely)

proposals.name: Dependence on a real-world calendar date or news cycle to parse
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet's sense depends on the reader knowing a specific real-world date, season, or contemporaneous news story (something that would go stale or become unintelligible outside a narrow real-world time window): 0 = fully intelligible with no dated or current-events context needed; 10 = unintelligible without knowing a specific date/news story. Score only this dependence, not whether the topical content is funny.
proposals.rationale: R37 ('Twerking Ever Since 2013 #July4thBirthday') is pinned to a specific calendar date, and R55 ('Cubs Win the World Series') and R20 ('We Were Always Great') depend on the reader tracking a specific real-world sports/political storyline at the time of posting; this dependence is a timing artifact that could be scored as clever topicality by one model without being intrinsic craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / topicality of production relative to real-world events

proposals.name: Explicit first-person authenticity or authority claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet explicitly asserts the author's own first-person identity, lived experience, or authenticity regarding the subject (words like 'I', 'actual', 'real', 'my own') as opposed to describing the subject in the third person with no personal claim: 0 = no first-person or authenticity claim; 10 = the tweet is built around an explicit first-person or authenticity assertion. Score only the presence of this self-referential claim, not whether it makes the tweet funnier.
proposals.rationale: R59 ('ACTUAL Sister Wives') and R39 ('I Speak 'Merican!') both foreground an explicit authenticity/first-person claim as their core move; this self-presentation tactic is a producer-side signal that could be rewarded independent of the joke's actual construction.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's self-presentation strategy / perceived-authenticity signaling practice

proposals.name: Raw character/word length of the tweet
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the tweet's raw length: 0 = extremely short (2-3 words), 10 = long and wordy (10+ words including the joke text). Score only length, never whether the length suits the joke.
proposals.rationale: The disagreement slice spans very short entries like R14 ('Tell you what.') and R40 ('Need To Get Out') to much longer ones like R56 ('What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?') and R28 ('16 Angry Men (and one woman)'); raw length is a classic surface proxy that either model could be latching onto independent of comedic merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Reference predictability / top-of-mind obviousness within its category
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how likely it is that many different people, independently and without seeing each other's answers, would land on the exact same reference the tweet uses (i.e. how canonical/first-guess the referenced title, phrase, or figure is for this prompt category): 0 = an obscure or highly idiosyncratic reference unlikely to be duplicated; 10 = the single most obvious, textbook reference for the category, of the kind many entrants would independently reach for. Score only this predictability, never whether the joke built on it is good.
proposals.rationale: R41 ('12 Angry Men : The Contenders') and R28 ('16 Angry Men (and one woman)') independently riff on the identical famous title, as do R38 ('Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie') and R08 ('Star Wars 7 With JarJar') on Star Wars/Jar Jar -- these duplications show the reference pool has crowded, highly-predictable landing spots; an item's position in the submission stream (how early/obvious a take it is) can leave this kind of trace without being a direct read on the entry's own craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / idea-crowding (obvious ideas get submitted first and are independently duplicated by many entrants, which can affect how fresh or stale a reader/judge perceives an entry as)

proposals.name: Title Reengineering Depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable title is transformed into a coherent, substantive new premise; score 0 when the change is merely a superficial name swap.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R19 turn familiar movie titles into specific political premises, unlike thinner title substitutions such as R28 and R35.

proposals.name: Morphological Wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a coined, blended, or altered word creates an immediate layered joke; score 0 when the wording contains no meaningful linguistic transformation.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R39 build compact jokes from uncledad and bruncle, showing word formation doing more work than ordinary phrases.

proposals.name: Distinctive Comic Voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds like a specific, recognizable comic speaker; score 0 when it is a generic phrase or interchangeable noun list.
proposals.rationale: R21 and R46 use conversational idioms that imply a vivid persona, whereas R29 and R52 read more like generic inventories.

proposals.name: Hashtag-Dependent Meaning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the central joke depends tightly on the stated hashtag premise; score 0 when the text would mean essentially the same thing under an unrelated hashtag.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R12 make America itself the subject of the joke, while R23 and R36 could function as generic redneck descriptions without the prompt.

proposals.name: Compressed Backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a few words imply a complete situation, relationship, or history; score 0 when the text supplies only an isolated label or disconnected image.
proposals.rationale: R49 implies an ominous history with the mother, and R30 implies a disturbing family scenario; both contain more latent narrative than simple labels such as R32.

proposals.name: Escalating Final Reveal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the ending sharply changes or intensifies the reader’s interpretation; score 0 when every word has the same predictable force from the start.
proposals.rationale: R49 gains menace from FOREVER, and R54 turns an accident into an unexpectedly bodily consequence, illustrating strong late-stage escalation.

proposals.name: Concrete Visuality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording produces a specific, memorable physical or sensory image; score 0 when it remains abstract, vague, or purely referential.
proposals.rationale: R42 supplies a highly tangible food image, and R50 makes beard flavor physically imaginable; these differ from abstract formulations such as R57.

proposals.name: Integrated List Coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every listed element compounds one coherent comic idea; score 0 when the words are merely topical keywords with no meaningful relation.
proposals.rationale: R29 and R52 present clusters of related terms that can be read as keyword piles, while the criterion tests whether their combination creates a unified joke.

proposals.name: Reference Recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural reference is placed in an unexpected context that changes its function; score 0 when the reference is only named or repeated without transformation.
proposals.rationale: R20 and R58 mainly invoke recognizable people or franchises, providing useful contrasts with more transformed references such as R06 and R38.

proposals.name: Fresh Angle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the premise approaches the hashtag through an unusual, non-default association; score 0 when it relies on the most familiar stereotype or stock phrase available.
proposals.rationale: R23 and R36 use conventional redneck associations, whereas fresher angles such as R07 and R39 approach the same prompt through inventive language.

proposals.name: Surface-Meaning Irony
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the literal wording clearly conflicts with an implied comic meaning; score 0 when the statement is straightforward and has no interpretive reversal.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R37 use affirmative or grammatical surfaces to suggest doubt about America, creating a meaningful gap between wording and implication.

proposals.name: Specific Ideological Contradiction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when political or cultural symbols are juxtaposed in a precise, surprising contradiction; score 0 when the text is only a generic partisan slogan or insult.
proposals.rationale: R40 and R55 combine political positions and redneck imagery into pointed contradictions, giving ideological tension more structure than R10’s direct insult.

proposals.name: Transgression With Comic Mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when taboo material is converted into humor through wordplay, framing, or an unexpected premise; score 0 when shock or offensiveness is the only apparent mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R15 and R30 rely heavily on incest or drugging premises, so this criterion distinguishes clever transgressive construction from mere provocation.

proposals.name: Genuine Scary-Story Unease
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text creates specific dread or unease appropriate to a scary story; score 0 when it merely names a celebrity, franchise, or ostensibly scary subject.
proposals.rationale: R48 and R49 turn familiar domestic situations into unsettling premises, unlike reference-driven entries such as R20 and R58.

proposals.name: Natural Phrasing Under Constraint
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the required short form remains idiomatic, grammatical, and effortlessly readable; score 0 when word-count compliance produces awkward syntax or a forced fragment.
proposals.rationale: R12, R21, and R46 show concise phrases that sound natural despite tight formats, providing a useful contrast with strained constructions such as R37.

proposals.name: Submission-wrapper convention
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the tweet follows a recurring hashtag/handle placement and spacing template; judge only this visible formatting pattern, not whether it is good or funny.
proposals.rationale: Posting habits or submission tools may leave consistent wrapper placement, which a text model can learn as a proxy. R10 places the handle and hashtag before the text, while R18 places both after it.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Link or media attachment
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of visible URL, media-pointer, or external-content residue; judge only its presence and prominence, not whether the linked material is good.
proposals.rationale: Cross-posting and attachment practices can create URL traces unrelated to the text's contest value. R23 and R28 contain shortened links, while R42 includes an external image link.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission workflow or cross-posting

proposals.name: Proper-noun reference density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet uses named people, franchises, films, institutions, or other recognizable entities; judge only reference density, not whether the references are effective.
proposals.rationale: A writer's repertoire and presumed audience can produce recognizable-reference fingerprints that models may use as shortcuts, while repertoire can also affect genuine writing ability. R04 names Jar Jar Binks, R16 names Bradley Cooper, and R17 invokes a film title.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's media repertoire and audience familiarity

proposals.name: Taboo vocabulary intensity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit sexual, drug-related, bodily, weapon, or similarly taboo vocabulary; judge only the lexical presence, not whether it improves the joke.
proposals.rationale: Taboo terms are conspicuous lexical signals that can attract model attention without constituting contest quality. R03 uses an incest reference, R11 uses Rohypnol, and R57 combines guns with abortion.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Partisan-political cue density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of explicit partisan, government, election, policy, or political-person vocabulary; judge only the topic cues, not whether the political framing is good.
proposals.rationale: Political vocabulary can trigger audience or model associations independently of construction quality. R17 uses GOP and agenda language, while R21, R22, and R32 use votes, healthcare, and Republican cues.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Vernacular orthography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of dialect spelling, nonstandard contractions, invented blends, or deliberately informal orthography; judge only these language-form choices, not whether they are amusing.
proposals.rationale: Repeated language habits can identify an author's community or practiced style, although those habits may also contribute to genuine expression. R07 uses uncledad, R08 uses bruncle, and R53 uses 'Merican.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice or identity signaling in the format

proposals.name: Stock phrase reuse
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the wording resembles a familiar slogan, catchphrase, idiom, or reusable template; judge only recognizability and reuse, not whether the phrase is effective.
proposals.rationale: Highly familiar phrasing supplies a memorability or corpus-frequency shortcut unrelated to intrinsic contest quality. R20 echoes a song phrase, R43 uses Gee, Thanks Obama, and R47 uses a commercial slogan.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Consumer-brand cue density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit brand, product, retail, or mass-consumer vocabulary; judge only the commercial or consumer references, not whether they are apt.
proposals.rationale: Commercially salient words may be disproportionately represented in learned associations without indicating quality. R13 names WalMart, R55 names Hostess Twinkie, and R58 stacks guns, NASCAR, and beer.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Obvious-first-take fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text reads as a default, immediately available association to the prompt, using familiar topical ingredients or a conventional premise; judge only those first-association cues, not originality or quality.
proposals.rationale: Early or crowded submission positions can encourage default prompt associations, leaving a textual trace even when actual position is unseen. R25 lists conventional redneck symbols, while R34 and R50 use direct, familiar prompt associations.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream or submission timing

proposals.name: Temporal anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit years, numbered installments, current-event references, or time-sensitive cultural anchors; judge only temporal specificity, not whether the reference is timely or good.
proposals.rationale: When an item is written relative to a news or cultural cycle, the timing may leave dated-reference fingerprints that models exploit independently of quality. R29 specifies 2013, R30 invokes the Cubs winning the World Series, and R10 names Star Wars VII.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and topical news cycle

proposals.name: Compressed Social Thesis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a few words combine concrete details into a pointed, coherent social observation; score 0 when they are merely an unconnected list or slogan.
proposals.rationale: R01 compresses Americana into an oligarchy critique, while R17 turns national pride into a compact historical claim.

proposals.name: Implied Setup
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording naturally sets up an unstated comic continuation or scene; score 0 when it is only a generic standalone phrase.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R09 sound like recognizable preambles whose implied next action supplies much of the humor.

proposals.name: Concrete Cultural Texture
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when specific objects, places, or practices create a vivid, culturally grounded world; score 0 when the entry relies only on vague labels.
proposals.rationale: R04 evokes a particular rural place, and R58 uses a tightly selected set of concrete regional details.

proposals.name: Ironic Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar phrase is redirected toward an unexpected comic meaning; score 0 when the phrase is used literally or without a new implication.
proposals.rationale: R03 repurposes a political catchphrase as a redneck response, and R19 gives a familiar lyric an ironic contextual meaning.

proposals.name: Word Fusion Precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a coined or blended word makes both source meanings immediately legible and creates a clear joke; score 0 when the alteration is confusing or merely misspelled.
proposals.rationale: R13 bruncle and R22 uncledad demonstrate compact word formation that joins family relationships with the prompt.

proposals.name: Instant Tableau
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the words immediately produce a specific, filmable comic image; score 0 when no distinct scene can be pictured.
proposals.rationale: R05 suggests a concrete action scene, while R51 turns a dog riding in a vehicle into an instantly visual premise.

proposals.name: Narrative Escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise sharply escalates into a disproportionate or unsettling endpoint; score 0 when there is no progression or surprise.
proposals.rationale: R18 escalates an accident into an embarrassing bodily consequence, and R47 turns a routine visit into an enduring threat.

proposals.name: Satirical Target Mechanics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry identifies a target and expresses a specific comic mechanism about it; score 0 when it is only a political label, affiliation, or insult.
proposals.rationale: R01 connects cultural symbols to oligarchy, and R35 links gun culture to a concrete political contradiction.

proposals.name: Prompt-Specific Angle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry fulfills the exact prompt through a fresh, unmistakable angle; score 0 when it is generic, loosely related, or merely repeats prompt vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R31 interpret the America prompt through distinct rhetorical stances rather than simple patriotic description.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke is understandable and complete from the text alone; score 0 when it depends on an external link, obscure reference, or missing context.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R54 require substantial familiarity with outside characters or media to supply the intended payoff.

proposals.name: Transformed Title Wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when altering a familiar title creates a new, specific, coherent premise; score 0 when it merely swaps one topical word into a recognizable title template.
proposals.rationale: R29 and R48 show title-based constructions whose humor depends heavily on the substitution pattern itself.

proposals.name: Stereotype Avoidance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry approaches the theme through an unusual, non-interchangeable detail; score 0 when it is an expected stereotype bundle that could fit almost any entry.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R34 use familiar redneck shorthand, making them useful contrasts for judging freshness beyond topical fit.

proposals.name: Spoken Cadence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording has a memorable rhythm, stress pattern, or repetition that would sound strong aloud; score 0 when it is rhythmically flat or awkward.
proposals.rationale: R16 has a compact, recognizable verbal cadence, while R55 uses deliberate repetition as its principal rhythmic device.

proposals.name: Recoverable Ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ambiguity supports two plausible readings and one yields a crisp comic interpretation; score 0 when ambiguity appears to be accidental confusion.
proposals.rationale: R42 and R45 both invite interpretation through unusual syntax or family-language ambiguity, making recoverability important to judge.

proposals.name: Transgressive Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when taboo or shocking material is integrated into a specific reversal, image, or narrative mechanism; score 0 when shock value is the entire joke.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R56 use highly transgressive premises whose quality depends on whether the taboo element does more than provoke.

proposals.name: Contest boilerplate load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the text consists of contest/platform boilerplate such as @midnight, the contest hashtag, or their repeated placement; judge visible boilerplate only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Submission-format habits can predict how an item is processed without describing its comic construction. Compare the packaging patterns in R01, R03, R08, and R47.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's familiarity with contest submission conventions

proposals.name: External-link trace
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the presence and prominence of URLs or linked-content cues; judge only the visible linking trace, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Links may signal cross-posting, promotion, or outside assistance rather than entry quality. This fingerprint appears in R03, R27, and R49.
proposals.upstream_parent: cross-posting or promotional workflow

proposals.name: Familiar-reference density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text relies on recognizable franchises, celebrities, characters, or widely known cultural properties; judge recognizability only, not whether the reference is good.
proposals.rationale: Shared reference knowledge can affect audience response independently of construction, while recognizability can also sometimes support genuine humor. Examples include R05, R14, R16, and R46.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience familiarity and shared cultural knowledge

proposals.name: Partisan-trigger density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains explicit partisan, ideological, or politically polarizing cues; judge cue intensity only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Political identity cues can attract or repel audiences for reasons unrelated to the line's craft. Visible examples include R11, R18, R41, R53, and R58.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience composition and political polarization

proposals.name: Stock-phrase residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the wording uses a familiar slogan, advertising line, title template, or circulating catchphrase; judge template familiarity only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Template familiarity may be predictive because readers recognize the source immediately, not because the entry is intrinsically better. Compare R02, R31, R47, and R58.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's reuse of culturally circulating templates

proposals.name: Morphological playfulness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of invented, fused, altered, or deliberately nonstandard words and spellings; judge the visible word formation only, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: A practiced wordplay style may influence how an author is perceived and may also genuinely affect construction, so this is a sensitivity channel. Examples are R25, R29, R34, R37, and R54.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice with wordplay and format

proposals.name: Taboo-trigger density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text invokes sex, drugs, bodily functions, violence, death, or other taboo material; judge taboo presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Taboo cues can change audience reaction or distribution independently of comic quality. They are visible in R12, R39, R50, and R51.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience norm sensitivity and platform-moderation climate

proposals.name: Dated-event anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text depends on a date, release installment, current figure, seasonal event, or time-bound public event; judge temporal anchoring only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Timing can make a reference salient or stale independently of wording quality, while topical relevance can also contribute genuinely to an entry. Examples include R04, R14, R46, R56, and R58.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and topical news cycle

proposals.name: First-association directness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the wording reads as an immediate, conventional association to the prompt, with little sign of a developed setup; judge directness only, not whether the association is good.
proposals.rationale: An early submission may leave a first-association fingerprint, while a later entrant may avoid already-obvious readings; stream position can therefore affect both nuisance patterns and substantive development. Compare R12, R31, R42, and R47.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Performed regional persona
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text performs a regional, class, occupational, or subcultural persona through dialect, lifestyle props, or identity markers; judge persona signaling only, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Persona signals can recruit an audience or reveal community membership independently of entry quality, although practiced familiarity with that persona may also shape genuinely effective writing. Examples include R07, R37, R48, R57, and R59.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's community identity, following, or practice in the format
